title: Range Module
statement:
Build a class `RangeModule` that keeps track of which real numbers are currently covered. Every range is half-open: `[left, right)` means all real numbers `x` with `left <= x < right`.

- `RangeModule()` starts with no numbers tracked.
- `addRange(left, right)` makes every number in `[left, right)` tracked; numbers there that were already tracked simply stay tracked.
- `queryRange(left, right)` returns `true` when every number in `[left, right)` is tracked at this moment, and `false` if any of them is not.
- `removeRange(left, right)` makes every number in `[left, right)` untracked; numbers outside that range are not affected.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls in total are made to addRange, queryRange and removeRange
notes:
## Intuition

The tracked numbers always form a union of intervals, so store that union directly: a list `intervals` of disjoint `[low, high)` pairs, sorted, with no two touching (touching ones are merged). One binary search, "the first interval whose end is at least `x`", answers every question. A query is covered only if a single stored interval contains it, and that interval must be the first one ending at or after `right`. Adding and removing only rewrite the run of intervals that overlap the new range, so each is a binary search plus one `splice`. (A simpler but slower model keeps every endpoint ever seen and a tracked flag for each piece between them.)

## Approach

1. `firstEndAtLeast(x)` binary-searches for the first interval with end `>= x`.
2. `addRange`: from `start = firstEndAtLeast(left)`, absorb every interval beginning at or before `right` (touching counts), widening `low` and `high`; replace that run with `[low, high]`.
3. `queryRange`: take `index = firstEndAtLeast(right)`; the answer is `true` exactly when that interval exists and starts at or before `left`.
4. `removeRange`: from `start = firstEndAtLeast(left)`, visit every interval starting before `right`; keep its part left of `left` and its part right of `right` as `pieces`, then splice them in place of the run.

## Example 1, step by step

`addRange(10, 20)` stores `[[10, 20]]`. `removeRange(14, 16)` visits `[10, 20]`: `10 < 14` keeps `[10, 14]` and `20 > 16` keeps `[16, 20]`, so `intervals = [[10, 14], [16, 20]]`. `queryRange(10, 14)`: the first interval ending at or after 14 is `[10, 14]`, which starts at `10 <= 10`: `true`. `queryRange(13, 15)`: the first ending at or after 15 is `[16, 20]`, which starts after 13: `false`. `queryRange(16, 17)` finds `[16, 20]`: `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: `queryRange` is O(log k); `addRange` and `removeRange` are O(log k + k) because of the splice, with k stored intervals.
- Space: O(k) for `intervals`.

## Pitfalls

- Ranges are half-open: `[1, 5)` and `[5, 10)` together cover `[1, 10)`, so merge intervals that only touch.
- After `removeRange(5, 6)` on `[1, 10)`, the number 5 is gone but 6 is still tracked.
- A query that straddles a gap must fail even if both ends are tracked; checking just the endpoints is wrong.
- Removing from an empty module, or a range with nothing tracked, must leave the module unchanged.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `intervals` | sorted, disjoint, non-touching tracked intervals `[low, high]` |
| `low`, `high` | bounds of the binary search, or of the interval being built or split |
| `start`, `end` | first and one-past-last index of the run of intervals being replaced |
| `x`, `mid` | the value searched for and the middle index being tested |
| `index` | the only interval that could contain a queried range |
| `pieces` | the parts of removed intervals that stay tracked |
